title: Phishing Forensics: dissect the email
description: Lying headers, spoofed HELO, SPF +all and malware attachments: dissect phishing emails like a SOC analyst.

1.title: Headers: who really sends
1.body:
## Reading an email from top to bottom

Download the suspicious email in raw form:

```bash
curl -s http://127.0.0.1:18106/emails/02-urgente.eml
```

Headers are read from the BOTTOM UP (each hop adds one on top).
The ones that give away the real sender:

| Header | What it tells you | In the phishing email |
|---|---|---|
| `Return-Path` | Where the email bounces to (the one who really sends it) | `corp-supplies.cn`, not a bank |
| `Received` | The HELO that greeted + the real IP | Says `banco-seguro` but the IP is a different one |
| `Message-ID` | Generated by the sending server | The attacker's domain |
| `Authentication-Results` | SPF/DKIM/DMARC according to the receiver | none/none/fail |
| `Reply-To` | Where YOUR reply goes | A `mail.ru` account |

The `From:` is the only thing the user sees — and it's the ONLY thing the attacker
controls 100%. That is **spoofing**: the visible address lies;
Return-Path, Received and Message-ID are emitted by the attacker's
infrastructure, and the attacker can't retouch them that easily.

## SPF/DKIM/DMARC in 30 seconds

- **SPF** (DNS TXT): "is the sending IP authorized by the From
  domain?" — `+all` authorizes everyone (useless), `-all` forbids everyone else.
- **DKIM**: cryptographic signature of the message, validates integrity + domain.
- **DMARC**: the policy on what to do if SPF/DKIM fail (`p=none` is
  "do nothing" — common and unfortunate).

```bash
curl -s "http://127.0.0.1:18106/check-spf?domain=banco-seguro.com"   # healthy
curl -s "http://127.0.0.1:18106/check-spf?domain=corp-supplies.cn"   # +all
```

The attacker picks domains with a useless SPF precisely so that their
messages get past the filters. That's why `spf=none` + `dmarc=fail` in the
Authentication-Results is a red flag, not a harmless error.

phishing-forensics-t01-q01.prompt: From 02-urgente.eml: the HELO claims mail.banco-seguro.com but lies. What is the REAL origin domain (check Return-Path and Message-ID)? Submit it to /verify?origin= for the flag.

phishing-forensics-t01-q02.prompt: Same email: Authentication-Results shows three failed checks. Write all three with their value, in this order and separated by commas: format 'spf=X,dkim=Y,dmarc=Z'.
phishing-forensics-t01-q02.hint: spf=none, dkim=none, dmarc=fail — copy them exactly from the header

phishing-forensics-t01-q03.prompt: The attacker domain's SPF record (check-spf) contains a policy that makes it useless. Which mechanism is it? Query /check-spf?domain=<attacker-domain> for the flag.
phishing-forensics-t01-q03.hint: v=spf1 +all authorizes ANY server in the world to send as that domain

2.title: The disguised URL and the attachment
2.body:
## The domain disguised as a subdomain

The most profitable phishing trick: putting the legitimate domain INSIDE
yours, as a subdomain:

```
http://banco-seguro.com.verify-login.cn:8080/session?...
      └─ they make you look here ─┘└── real domain ───┘
```

The eye reads "banco-seguro.com" and approves; the resolver asks for
`verify-login.cn`. Variants of the same trick: `verify-banco.com`,
`banco-seguro-cuenta.com`, homoglyphs (`bancо` with a Cyrillic о), and URLs
with `@` (everything before the @ is a username: `http://banco.com@evil.cn/`).

```bash
curl -s http://127.0.0.1:18106/emails/02-urgente.eml | grep -A1 "clic"
# write down domain + port and validate them:
curl -s "http://127.0.0.1:18106/verify?url=banco-seguro.com.verify-login.cn:8080"
```

**Lesson for the defender**: extract the eTLD+1 (the registrable site)
with Public Suffix List (PSL) libraries before comparing strings; for the user: teach them to
read from right to left up to the first slash.

## The attachment: the one that does the damage

The URL steals credentials; the attachment (a .zip here, .doc macros in
real life) delivers the malware. In the MIME it travels in the second part:

```
Content-Type: application/zip; name="Detalles_de_la_incidencia.zip"
Content-Disposition: attachment; filename="Detalles_de_la_incidencia.zip"
```

The indicators of compromise (IOCs) an analyst records from this
email: the Return-Path domain, the Received IP, the URL domain,
the port, the attachment filename and its SHA256 hash. With that data the SOC
blocks at the mail gateway and hunts for other recipients.

## The pressure triad

Urgency (24h), authority (your bank), fear (account deleted). If an
email rushes you, that IS the signal: no legitimate organization puts you on
the clock. Reporting that pattern — not just this email — is what turns an
isolated incident into a detected campaign.

phishing-forensics-t02-q01.prompt: The email 02 link says 'banco-seguro.com' but points elsewhere. What is the real domain (with port)? Submit it to /verify?url= for the flag.
phishing-forensics-t02-q01.hint: The href is http://banco-seguro.com.<REAL-DOMAIN>:8080/... — the bank is a SUBDOMAIN of the attacker's domain

phishing-forensics-t02-q02.prompt: What is the attachment's exact filename (Content-Disposition)? Submit it to /verify?attachment= for the flag.
phishing-forensics-t02-q02.hint: MIME multipart: the second part declares application/zip with filename=...

phishing-forensics-t02-q03.prompt: Besides URL and attachment, the email uses 3 social-pressure techniques. Which one imposes a deadline to act?
phishing-forensics-t02-q03.hint: "Your account will be suspended in 24h unless you verify immediately": what feeling does that deadline create?
